name: which realism effects change a flood vehicle stability verdict
goal: My simulation of a vehicle in floodwater produces a binary engineering verdict: whether the vehicle begins to move or stays put. I have limited supercomputer time and I want to spend it on physical realism that actually changes that verdict rather than on realism that only improves how the result looks. I need the literature ranked by measured effect on an incipient motion or flotation threshold, with the effect size and its source, and I need to be told plainly where nobody has measured it. The specific effects I care about are these. First, road surface geometry: camber, crown, gutter, kerb and longitudinal grade, and whether anyone has demonstrated that a crowned or cambered road changes a vehicle stability threshold compared with a flat plane. My computational cell is about 0.15 metres and real road surface texture depth is a few millimetres, roughly one fiftieth of a cell. Second, free surface fidelity: air entrainment, spray formation, surface tension and turbulence closure. Third, water compressibility: I use a reduced bulk modulus giving a numerical sound speed around 13 metres per second, which is below the common guideline that it should exceed ten times the maximum flow velocity. Fourth, outlet boundary conditions for free surface particle methods. Fifth, vehicle watertightness and underbody detail.
summary:
Road/tyre friction and vehicle watertightness have the clearest demonstrated power to change a flood-stability verdict; slope and flow orientation also matter, whereas NO RETRIEVED STUDY QUANTIFIES A CROWNED OR CAMBERED ROAD AGAINST A FLAT PLANE [Smi19, Kra16, Azh23, Mil20, Boc19].

EFFECTS WITH THRESHOLD EVIDENCE.
- Bed condition/friction: full-scale tests measured traction on concrete, gravel, and sand and found materially different friction coefficients, requiring a worst-case value; SPH rough-bed studies validate velocity and shear-stress fields, but do not report a vehicle motion-threshold shift or a resolved-versus-effective-roughness error [Smi19, Kaz16, Kaz20, Shi19].
- Road slope/orientation: a conceptual model includes terrain slope, and experiments show stability depends on flow angle; a 5% grade study reports buoyancy onset at 0.055 m model depth, not a flat-road comparison [Mil20, Kra16, Sha19d].
- Watertightness: watertight models produce higher floating depths at prototype scale, while reviewed stability thresholds vary substantially with watertightness; no retrieved source isolates a sealed-versus-flooding threshold difference in metres [Kra16, Boc19].
- Unsteady free surface: simulated drag rises 40-50% under accelerating flow, but this is not a discrete verdict comparison [Azh26].

EFFECTS WITHOUT A DEMONSTRATED VERDICT SHIFT. No retrieved study shows air entrainment, spray, surface tension, turbulence closure, reduced sound speed, or outlet-boundary choice flipping vehicle motion. Compressibility papers document wave/impact sensitivity, not a move/no-move flip; THE TEN-TIMES-FLOW-SPEED RULE HAS NO PRIMARY DERIVATION HERE [Dal07, Vic12, Sdi00]. SPH outlet studies provide characteristic, buffer, pressure, and traction formulations, but do not establish a minimum sufficient condition for steady discharge or vehicle stability [Las09, Vac12, Neg19, Taf18, Hol20].
